source_reviews.independent_solution: Inherit the frozen independent source solution without solving it again or reopening images. The drawing establishes an approximately horizontal crossbar and structure, not incident direction, polarization or matching, so actual B direction is not unique. Ideal electric-dipole voltage depends on axial E projection; nonzero reception does not prove full polarization matching. Under the far-field free-space plane-wave model B=(n cross E)/c, with x along an assumed physical horizontal rod and z vertical. Matched linear E=x and n=y give B=-z; matched E=x and n=(y+z)/sqrt(2) give B along (y-z)/sqrt(2), not vertical. Horizontal n=y with E along (x+z)/sqrt(2) still excites the rod but gives B along (x-z)/sqrt(2). Vertical B therefore requires explicit horizontal-rod/matching/horizontal-transverse-propagation assumptions rather than the picture alone.

mathematics.independent_solution: The new hypothetical fields were solved from the view and recorded before key disclosure: B_I=(E0/c)cos(phi)(x-z)/sqrt(2), fixed tilted-line oscillation; B_II=(E0/c)[x sin(phi)-z cos(phi)], rotation in xz, pointing -z at phi=0 and x at phi=pi/2. Axial voltage is proportional to E0 cos(phi)/sqrt(2) for I and E0 cos(phi) for II. With E0>0 and omega>0 both are non-identically-zero AC. Only C satisfies all claims.
